fr:title.text: How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Intuitive walkthrough of Lean/LambekD/LinearElab/ — how a surface term like

gets turned into a morphism \llbracket {A \otimes B}\rrbracket _\ell \to A \otimes B in an abstract monoidal / biclosed / (co)cartesian / indexed / inductive category \mathcal {C}. Meant to be read alongside the code, not as a spec.

The elaborator is a syntax-to-syntax preprocessor. It does not manufacture Lean Exprs itself; instead it reads a DSL expression, decides for each subterm which typed combinator should stand in for it, and builds a Lean source-level term that applies those combinators. The generated source is handed back to Lean's normal elabTerm at the very end. Unification, typeclass resolution, and universe inference happen once, there, on the full tree — not piecewise while we are walking the DSL.
Conceptually:

html:ul.html:li: DSL syntax (category lterm) lives in LinearElab/Syntax.lean. Each connective of the paper has its own shape: (x, y), let (a,b) = _ in _, fun (x:A) =>, ⟨e₁, e₂⟩, match _ with | inl a => _ | inr b => _, and so on.

Combinators live in LambekD.Linear.{Monoidal,Biclosed, Cartesian,Cocartesian,IndexedProducts,IndexedCoproducts,Inductive}. Each is a plain Lean definition parametric in a category \mathcal {C} carrying only the structure that connective needs (monoidal, left- closed, right-closed, chosen products, chosen coproducts, chosen distributor, initial algebras). No reference to Grammar.

The elaborator in LinearElab/Elaborator.lean is the bridge: one partial def per DSL form, emitting a TSyntax `term that mentions exactly the right combinator with exactly the right context arguments pinned down.

fr:title.text: What the combinators want from us

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What the combinators want from us

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Take tensorIntro as representative:
tensorIntro (e₁ : ⟦Δ⟧ₗ ⟶ A) (e₂ : ⟦Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ B) : ⟦Δ ++ Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ A ⊗ B (with Δ, Δ', A, B implicit).

LinCtx C is an ordered left-to-right list of \mathcal {C}-objects (think: a telescope of linear types). ⟦_⟧ₗ folds it into a right-nested tensor. The combinator takes two morphisms, on contexts Δ and Δ', and returns a morphism on the concatenated context Δ ++ Δ'.

So when the user writes (e₁, e₂) with ambient context \Delta _{\text {full}}, there is exactly one decision to make: where to cut \Delta _{\text {full}} into a prefix \Delta used by e₁ and a suffix \Delta ' used by e₂. The rest — what A, B, and \mathcal {C} are — is Lean's problem.

Every other combinator is the same pattern. Some take one context (var, unitIntro, prodIntro, sumInl); some take a middle slice and an outer prefix + suffix (unitElim, tensorElim, sumElim, coprodDElim, botElim); the rest are binders that add or remove a single slot at the front or the end (limpRIntro, limpLIntro, funD). The elaborator's job is to look at the DSL shape, compute the cuts, and emit the corresponding combinator applied to its inputs with the cuts threaded through explicitly.

fr:title.text: The cutting algorithm: free variables and ordering

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The cutting algorithm: free variables and ordering

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two tiny helpers do almost all the work.

html:ul.html:li: freeVars : TSyntax `lterm → Array Name — purely syntactic, recurses through the term and collects identifiers that are not shadowed by a binder. It knows about all the DSL's binding forms (let () = _ in, let (a,b) = _ in, fun (x:T) =>, funl (x:T) =>, match _ with | inl a | inr b, matchD _ with | ⟪x, y⟫).

splitCtx fvLeft fvRight — walks the ambient context left-to-right and finds the unique split point i such that the first i names lie in fvLeft and the rest in fvRight. Throws an error if any variable is unused, reused across branches, or appears out of order.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For middle-slice forms (let (a,b) = e in e' and friends) there is a second helper splitCtxMiddle fvMid fvOuter that finds a contiguous range of indices all of whose variables lie in fvMid, asserts that range really is contiguous, and returns the three pieces \Delta '_1, \Delta , \Delta '_2 around it.

These two functions enforce ordered linearity — no contraction (variable appearing twice on the same side of a split), no weakening (a variable that goes nowhere), no exchange (a left-variable appearing after a right-variable). When the user-written binder structure of the DSL does not support a valid cut, splitCtx itself raises the error. The main loop never has to think about linearity; it only asks "where does the cut go?" and delegates.

Cartesian and indexed-product intro are the only forms that do not cut: ⟨e₁, e₂⟩ shares the whole ambient context between the two branches (cartesian is additive, so it permits the same resources to be used by both). The elaborator simply recurses on each branch with the full ctx and lets the branches' internal linearity checks enforce that each branch really does consume it.

fr:title.text: The unification subtlety — why we pin Δ with named arguments

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The unification subtlety — why we pin Δ with named arguments

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Combinators like tensorIntro type as ⟦Δ ++ Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ A ⊗ B. When we apply such a combinator to a concrete ambient context \Delta _{\text {full}}, Lean's unifier tries to solve Δ ++ Δ' = Δ_full. That equation has many solutions (any cut point works), and because LinCtx.append recurses on its right argument, Lean's unifier eagerly pins \Delta ' to some small suffix and leaves \Delta as whatever is left — typically not the split our FV analysis computed.
To stop Lean from guessing, the elaborator serialises the exact cut pieces back into surface syntax:

html:p.html:code: ctxToSyntax vars = nil.snoc A₀.snoc A₁. ⋯ .snoc A_k

fr:mainmatter.html:p: and passes them to the combinator as named implicit arguments ((Δ := $Δstx) / (Δ' := $Δ'stx)). Now when Lean sees tensorIntro (Δ := A,B) (Δ' := C,D) m₁ m₂, both halves are syntactically pinned and the equation (A,B) ++ (C,D) = A,B,C,D reduces definitionally. No unification ambiguity remains.
The same trick is what unblocks middle-slice combinators (unitElim, tensorElim, sumElim, coprodDElim, botElim), which have two append patterns in their types.
x ⟶ Linear.var A: singleton context [(x, A)] maps by identity into the slot.
() ⟶ Linear.unitIntro: requires empty context, produces the monoidal unit I.
(e₁, e₂) ⟶ tensorIntro (Δ := …) (Δ' := …) m₁ m₂: splitCtx (FV e₁) (FV e₂) picks the cut; each branch is elaborated in its own piece of the context.

let () = e in e' and let (a,b) = e in e': e consumes a middle slice Δ, e' runs on Δ'₁ ++ Δ'₂ (plus the new binders in the pair case). We emit unitElim / tensorElim with the three pieces pinned. The new binders in the pair case get hole types _; Lean fills them from the type of e.

Ordinary functions come in two flavours because context is ordered. fun (x : A) => e pushes x onto the end of the ambient ctx and emits limpRIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing A →[C] B. funl (x : A) => e pushes it onto the front and emits limpLIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing B [C]← A. The ambient ctx is passed as Δ so that Lean does not try to solve Δ.snoc A = newCtx or sole A ++ Δ = newCtx by guessing.

Application likewise splits into two rules by which side the function appears on. f a (juxtaposition, function on the left) is limpRApp; a ·⟜ f (argument on the left) is limpLApp. The two combinators have their append patterns in opposite orders (Δ ++ Δ' vs Δ' ++ Δ), so the elaborator has to know which side is the function when it emits the call.

Additive, so there is no cut: ⟨e₁, e₂⟩ elaborates both branches under the same ambient context, and Lean's A \amp B constructor uses the cartesian lift combinator. ⟨⟩ is the unique morphism into the chosen terminal and accepts any ambient ctx. Projections just post-compose with fst or snd.
Injections are pre-composed with inl / inr — no cut.

match e with | inl a => f | inr b => g is the only genuinely subtle monoidal case outside tensor-elim. The scrutinee e consumes a contiguous middle slice \Delta , and both branches share the outer context \Delta '_1, \Delta '_2, each extending it with one new binder (a or b, with hole types filled from e's type). Emission is sumElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m mf mg; the underlying combinator bakes in the distributor so that the two branches of the coproduct really do glue back into a single morphism on the whole ambient ctx.

absurd e is \bot -elim. The scrutinee provides a morphism into the initial object; the distributor's annihilation maps any flanking context to the initial. That means we are allowed to have ambient variables that do not appear in e at all — they just get annihilated. In freeVars this breaks the usual "every variable must be used somewhere" invariant, so the elaborator special-cases absurd: ambient vars outside FV(e) are treated as "used by the annihilation", not as an unused-variable error.

funD (x : X) => e introduces a non-linear (Lean-level) binder x : X that the body can mention as an ordinary Lean term but not as a linear variable. The linear context is unchanged for the body — nothing is consumed. The elaborator elaborates e under the same ambient ctx, then wraps the result in a Lean fun x : X => _ and hands that to prodDIntro, which is exactly the liftD of the chosen indexed-product structure.
e ·@ x post-composes the projection at index x.
⟪x, e⟫ injects at a specified index; coprodDInj x e.

matchD e with | ⟪x, y⟫ => body: like match, e consumes a middle slice and body gets one new linear binder y (with a hole type inferred from the index family) and one non-linear binder x : X. Emission is coprodDElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m (fun x => body), where the fun x => … captures the non-linear binder from the surface syntax.

roll[x] e is muRoll _ x e, which is literally e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.roll x: post-compose the linear body with the initial algebra's constructor at index x. The _ is a placeholder for the functor F, which Lean is expected to recover from the expected return type \mu F x.

fold[algs] e is muFold algs e = e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.fold algs x: post-compose with the catamorphism induced by the algebra algs : ∀ y, (F y).denote A ⟶ A y. roll and fold do not restructure the context; they just chain on top of it.

The \beta and \eta laws of initial algebras (fold_roll, fold_unique) are semantic lemmas, not judgmental — the elaborator does nothing to expose them, it is up to the programmer to rewrite when needed.
The top-level macro in elabLinearBracket:

html:ol.html:li: Reads the surface syntax (x₁ : A₁) … (xₙ : Aₙ) => body.
Builds the initial ElabCtx from the typed binders: an array of (Name × TSyntax `term) pairs, in the order written.

Runs the elaborator elabLTerm body under that context. The output is a single TSyntax `term — a Lean source-level term mentioning Linear.tensorIntro, Linear.sumElim, etc., with all context pieces and non-linear binders wired up.

Calls Lean.Elab.Term.elabTerm on that syntax with the expected type from the surrounding Lean context. Unification and typeclass resolution — for the category \mathcal {C} itself, for the types of the binders, for the appropriate chosen-structure instances — all happen here, once, on the finished tree.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The elaborator never inspects Expr, never calls isDefEq, never synthesises an instance. It is a syntactic preprocessor that knows how to name the right combinators and pin their context implicits; everything semantic is Lean's job.

html:ul.html:li: No escape hatch #[f] to embed a Lean-level morphism. The grammar-specific Elab/ elaborator has one; the linear one does not — if you need to use a Lean-constructed morphism, you must currently write the term directly (as in the prodDIntro smoke test which falls back to the raw combinator).
No constructor-apps for grammar_inductive-style named data. The inductive surface here is only the roll/fold pair.
No match … with on μ F beyond what fold expresses, and no equivalent of the grammar_decreasing termination plumbing. Both were grammar-specific in the older elaborator.
No Lean-level rewrite / simp hooks; β/η laws of each connective exist as simp lemmas on the combinators, but the DSL does not surface them.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are all deliberate omissions — the LinearElab elaborator is the minimal, category-polymorphic core. The grammar-specific pieces live in the older Elab/ tree and compose with these combinators via instances on Grammar.

html:ul.html:li: sss-009P Lean port of the surface elaborator — umbrella plan under which this work sits.
sss-009U Parameterize the elaborator over the target category — this tree documents the result of that task.
sss-009V Validate genericity in a non-grammars category — the next step: exercise these combinators in a non-grammars instance.

fr:title.text: PhD roadmap: Dependent Lambek Calculus as the central object

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: PhD roadmap: Dependent Lambek Calculus as the central object

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two-year sketch. Expansion of the PhD-roadmap section of the 2026-05-13 meeting prep, drafted for discussion with Max. Replaces the one-paragraph sketch there.

Thesis claim. Dependent Lambek Calculus (DLC) is the central object of the dissertation. DLC is developed along three coupled axes: categorical-semantic metatheory (via displayed categories), algorithmic content (compositional characterizations of practical parsing algorithms), and implementation (a Lean tool usable enough to host real-language parser correctness proofs). The synthesis chapter is self-hosted parser correctness for the Lean and Agda frontends, written inside the host languages themselves.

Why the three axes are one PhD, not three. The displayed-categorical machinery makes the parsing-theoretic content mechanizable; the parsing-theoretic content motivates and stress-tests the foundational machinery; the Lean implementation is what makes the correctness claims executable on real proof-assistant frontends. Strictification (Strictification) cuts across as the enabling technique for mechanization.

Paper 1: Logical Relations on Display. In flight; target submission in ~3 months. Establishes the displayed-categorical framework that downstream papers use to mechanize DLC metatheorems. Gated by the conservativity rewrite and the formalization-slowness fix; tracked at the paper milestone. The strictification technique (Yoneda Strictification: Tradeoffs and Opportunities, Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories) is a likely auxiliary section.

Paper 2: LL(1) parsing in Dependent Lambek Calculus (with Max and Cass; target ~6–9 months). Characterize LL(1) parsers in DLC compositionally; derive a parser-generator algorithm from the characterization. Two critical claims from the 2026-04-22 meeting: recursive-descent parsers are unfolds, not folds, and the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra (Cass's lever — verify against [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] early). The derivative-based plan and its brzozowski-branch execution track supply the syntactic machinery (Brzozowski derivatives as the linear residual \multimap , decidable nullability, the amazing right adjoint). The regular-grammar precursor is deterministic regex → LL(1). Well-founded recursion is the recursion principle of record; guarded recursion ▷ / Löb, tracked at the well-founded-recursion milestone, remains as a fallback if Cass's lever does not transport to the substructural setting. Likely venue: POPL / ICFP / LICS.

Paper 3: Richer parsing classes and a usable Lean tool (target ~12–15 months). Generalize Paper 2's characterization to LL(k) and LR; fold in the Chu / GL-reduct treatment of parsers with structured failure (PEG, negative lookahead) via the recursive-coalgebra synthesis. The Lean port of the elaborator lands as a real tool — LinearElab already works for the linear core; the new development is the grammar-specific extensions and a parser-generation backend. Demonstrate on a non-trivial language fragment (an expression-language or JSON-class target). Likely venue: PLDI tools / ICFP / CPP.

Paper 4: Self-hosting parser correctness for Lean and Agda (target ~18–24 months; defense chapter). Encode the actual parser of Lean (resp. Agda) inside DLC, within Lean (resp. Agda) itself; prove correctness theorems against the language spec. This is the synthesis: it brings together Paper 1's metatheory, Papers 2–3's parsing characterizations, and Paper 3's implementation. Scope risk acknowledged — if lifting to both host languages overruns, narrow to one (Lean is the better-resourced bet given the existing LinearElab port). Likely venue: POPL / a top-tier journal / CPP / ITP.

Paper 5 (stretch): Transition-system verification by gluing. Apply the displayed-categorical-logic framework off-axis — glue over the free category of a distributed system's labelled transition system to extract safety / liveness proofs for mutex-class algorithms. Concrete and applications-flavored; slots in between any of Papers 2–4 if scheduling permits. Likely venue: CAV / CONCUR / verification.

html:p.html:strong: Side threads (not required for the PhD).

html:ul.html:li: DLC metatheorems via cubical-categorical-logic. Likely absorbed into the chapter for Paper 2 or Paper 4 as "we mechanize the following DLC metatheorems using our own logical-relations framework" rather than its own paper.
CBPV (or similar richer TT) metatheory. Eric Bond is working in this direction — collaboration opportunity, more naturally post-PhD or as a final-chapter sketch than a core chapter.
Locally-small / large category theory in Agda. Infrastructure for cubical-categorical-logic. Possible tools / library paper, but not a core chapter.
Practical transition-system verification. See Paper 5 above if it gets promoted from side thread.
Fuller 2-category library in Agda. Pure infrastructure; absorbed into the cubical-categorical-logic library where needed.
Displayed categories — under Paper 1 (logical relations) and Paper 4 (DLC metatheory).

Recursive coalgebras / well-founded recursion — under Papers 2–4. Cass's lever (Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra) is critical for Paper 2; verify early.

Strictification (Yoneda Strictification: Tradeoffs and Opportunities, Cayley strictification of grammars: StrictGrammar = Grammar → Grammar, Cayley strictification of a monoidal category, Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories) — enabling tool for Papers 1 and 2 rather than a standalone paper, unless the methodology grows.
Lean implementation (How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms) — foundation for Papers 3 and 4; needs grammar-specific extensions beyond the current linear core.
Brzozowski derivatives + amazing right adjoint — concrete syntactic machinery for Paper 2, currently on the brzozowski worktree.
Guarded recursion ▷ / Löb (State and Attempt Löb Induction for ▷, ▷ as a Later Modality from Tiny Strings) — fallback recursion principle if the recursive-coalgebra story doesn't transport.
P1 (3 mo) — risk: conservativity rewrite or speed fix overruns; impact bounded by absorbing strictification as the rescue.
P2 (6–9 mo) — risk: Cass's lever doesn't transport. Mitigation: front-load verification of the lever; fall back to guarded recursion as plan B.

P3 (12–15 mo) — risk: LinearElab ergonomics are inadequate for non-trivial languages. Mitigation: keep the target language modest (expression languages, JSON-class) rather than push to a full programming language inside this paper.
P4 (18–24 mo) — risk: scope blow-up. Mitigation: narrow to one host language (Lean) if both is too much.
Does DLC metatheory absorb into Paper 4, or warrant its own chapter (possibly Paper 4.5)?
Is the Chu / PEG story a Paper 3 fold-in or a separate paper?
Strictification — paper or technique? Standalone methods paper, or absorbed into Papers 1 and 2?
How to budget the Eric Bond / CBPV thread — final-chapter sketch, collaboration in parallel, or strictly post-PhD?
Defense timing for a 24-month horizon — does the schedule above support a Spring 2028 defense, and what does that imply for proposal / candidacy timing?

fr:title.text: Validate genericity in a non-grammars category

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Validate genericity in a non-grammars category

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Once Parameterize the elaborator over the target category lands, exercise the generic interface by elaborating the same surface DSL into at least one non-grammars instance — candidates include a free monoidal biclosed category, a presheaf category \hat {\mathcal {C}} on some small \mathcal {C}, or a syntactic category from a different domain.

The point is to catch leakage of grammars-specific assumptions (e.g. concatenation, splittings, String indexing) that the abstract interface failed to hide. Examples should be small but should hit each connective.

fr:title.text: Parameterize the elaborator over the target category

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parameterize the elaborator over the target category

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current sketch hardwires the target: Grammar = String → Type, A ⊢ B = ∀ w, A w → B w, tensor as splittings, etc. Refactor so the elaborator emits terms in an abstract categorical interface — a typeclass packaging the structure required by each connective (monoidal biclosed, finite (co)products, indexed (co)products, initial algebras for grammar_inductive, the LNL adjunction once Embed the full linear / non-linear DSL lands, etc.).

Recover the existing grammars semantics as one instance of this interface. Track exactly which connectives need which structure so users can elaborate fragments of the DSL in categories that don't satisfy the full bill.

Read ~/grammars-and-semantic-actions/Lean/LambekD/Elab/ end-to-end and produce a written summary covering: surface syntax categories (gterm, gpat), the OrderedCtx discipline, how findSplit and the application-resolution rules are implemented, and what Elaborator.lean actually emits for each surface form.

fr:title.text: Lean Implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lean Implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal: a Lean 4 implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus whose surface syntax mirrors the on-paper presentation and elaborates, via Lean's extensible elaboration and metaprogramming, into the denotational semantics. The implementation should faithfully realize the full linear / non-linear calculus and be generic enough to evaluate the syntax in any category with sufficient structure — not solely the category of grammars.

Starting point. A Claude-written sketch lives in ~/grammars-and-semantic-actions/Lean/ (root LambekD.lean, elaborator under LambekD/Elab/, ~3.7k lines). It compiles and has working [| ... |] elaboration for the ordered linear fragment plus a grammar_inductive command. It is unaudited: the syntax/semantics correspondence and the design of the elaborator are not yet fully understood or owned. Treat it as scaffolding, not as a finished implementation.

html:ul.html:li: An elaboration pipeline from the on-paper Lambek^D syntax into Lean terms that I understand end-to-end and can extend.
An embedded DSL for the full linear / non-linear calculus (not just the ordered linear fragment).

An abstraction of the elaborator over the target category, so that the same surface syntax can be interpreted in any sufficiently structured category — recovering the grammars instance as one example.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The unification subtlety — why we pin Δ with named arguments

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Combinators like tensorIntro type as ⟦Δ ++ Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ A ⊗ B. When we apply such a combinator to a concrete ambient context \Delta _{\text {full}}, Lean's unifier tries to solve Δ ++ Δ' = Δ_full. That equation has many solutions (any cut point works), and because LinCtx.append recurses on its right argument, Lean's unifier eagerly pins \Delta ' to some small suffix and leaves \Delta as whatever is left — typically not the split our FV analysis computed.
To stop Lean from guessing, the elaborator serialises the exact cut pieces back into surface syntax:

html:p.html:code: ctxToSyntax vars = nil.snoc A₀.snoc A₁. ⋯ .snoc A_k

fr:mainmatter.html:p: and passes them to the combinator as named implicit arguments ((Δ := $Δstx) / (Δ' := $Δ'stx)). Now when Lean sees tensorIntro (Δ := A,B) (Δ' := C,D) m₁ m₂, both halves are syntactically pinned and the equation (A,B) ++ (C,D) = A,B,C,D reduces definitionally. No unification ambiguity remains.
The same trick is what unblocks middle-slice combinators (unitElim, tensorElim, sumElim, coprodDElim, botElim), which have two append patterns in their types.
x ⟶ Linear.var A: singleton context [(x, A)] maps by identity into the slot.
() ⟶ Linear.unitIntro: requires empty context, produces the monoidal unit I.
(e₁, e₂) ⟶ tensorIntro (Δ := …) (Δ' := …) m₁ m₂: splitCtx (FV e₁) (FV e₂) picks the cut; each branch is elaborated in its own piece of the context.

let () = e in e' and let (a,b) = e in e': e consumes a middle slice Δ, e' runs on Δ'₁ ++ Δ'₂ (plus the new binders in the pair case). We emit unitElim / tensorElim with the three pieces pinned. The new binders in the pair case get hole types _; Lean fills them from the type of e.

Ordinary functions come in two flavours because context is ordered. fun (x : A) => e pushes x onto the end of the ambient ctx and emits limpRIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing A →[C] B. funl (x : A) => e pushes it onto the front and emits limpLIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing B [C]← A. The ambient ctx is passed as Δ so that Lean does not try to solve Δ.snoc A = newCtx or sole A ++ Δ = newCtx by guessing.

Application likewise splits into two rules by which side the function appears on. f a (juxtaposition, function on the left) is limpRApp; a ·⟜ f (argument on the left) is limpLApp. The two combinators have their append patterns in opposite orders (Δ ++ Δ' vs Δ' ++ Δ), so the elaborator has to know which side is the function when it emits the call.

Additive, so there is no cut: ⟨e₁, e₂⟩ elaborates both branches under the same ambient context, and Lean's A \amp B constructor uses the cartesian lift combinator. ⟨⟩ is the unique morphism into the chosen terminal and accepts any ambient ctx. Projections just post-compose with fst or snd.
Injections are pre-composed with inl / inr — no cut.

match e with | inl a => f | inr b => g is the only genuinely subtle monoidal case outside tensor-elim. The scrutinee e consumes a contiguous middle slice \Delta , and both branches share the outer context \Delta '_1, \Delta '_2, each extending it with one new binder (a or b, with hole types filled from e's type). Emission is sumElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m mf mg; the underlying combinator bakes in the distributor so that the two branches of the coproduct really do glue back into a single morphism on the whole ambient ctx.

absurd e is \bot -elim. The scrutinee provides a morphism into the initial object; the distributor's annihilation maps any flanking context to the initial. That means we are allowed to have ambient variables that do not appear in e at all — they just get annihilated. In freeVars this breaks the usual "every variable must be used somewhere" invariant, so the elaborator special-cases absurd: ambient vars outside FV(e) are treated as "used by the annihilation", not as an unused-variable error.

funD (x : X) => e introduces a non-linear (Lean-level) binder x : X that the body can mention as an ordinary Lean term but not as a linear variable. The linear context is unchanged for the body — nothing is consumed. The elaborator elaborates e under the same ambient ctx, then wraps the result in a Lean fun x : X => _ and hands that to prodDIntro, which is exactly the liftD of the chosen indexed-product structure.
e ·@ x post-composes the projection at index x.
⟪x, e⟫ injects at a specified index; coprodDInj x e.

matchD e with | ⟪x, y⟫ => body: like match, e consumes a middle slice and body gets one new linear binder y (with a hole type inferred from the index family) and one non-linear binder x : X. Emission is coprodDElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m (fun x => body), where the fun x => … captures the non-linear binder from the surface syntax.

roll[x] e is muRoll _ x e, which is literally e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.roll x: post-compose the linear body with the initial algebra's constructor at index x. The _ is a placeholder for the functor F, which Lean is expected to recover from the expected return type \mu F x.

fold[algs] e is muFold algs e = e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.fold algs x: post-compose with the catamorphism induced by the algebra algs : ∀ y, (F y).denote A ⟶ A y. roll and fold do not restructure the context; they just chain on top of it.

The \beta and \eta laws of initial algebras (fold_roll, fold_unique) are semantic lemmas, not judgmental — the elaborator does nothing to expose them, it is up to the programmer to rewrite when needed.
The top-level macro in elabLinearBracket:

html:ol.html:li: Reads the surface syntax (x₁ : A₁) … (xₙ : Aₙ) => body.
Builds the initial ElabCtx from the typed binders: an array of (Name × TSyntax `term) pairs, in the order written.

Runs the elaborator elabLTerm body under that context. The output is a single TSyntax `term — a Lean source-level term mentioning Linear.tensorIntro, Linear.sumElim, etc., with all context pieces and non-linear binders wired up.

Calls Lean.Elab.Term.elabTerm on that syntax with the expected type from the surrounding Lean context. Unification and typeclass resolution — for the category \mathcal {C} itself, for the types of the binders, for the appropriate chosen-structure instances — all happen here, once, on the finished tree.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The elaborator never inspects Expr, never calls isDefEq, never synthesises an instance. It is a syntactic preprocessor that knows how to name the right combinators and pin their context implicits; everything semantic is Lean's job.

html:ul.html:li: No escape hatch #[f] to embed a Lean-level morphism. The grammar-specific Elab/ elaborator has one; the linear one does not — if you need to use a Lean-constructed morphism, you must currently write the term directly (as in the prodDIntro smoke test which falls back to the raw combinator).
No constructor-apps for grammar_inductive-style named data. The inductive surface here is only the roll/fold pair.
No match … with on μ F beyond what fold expresses, and no equivalent of the grammar_decreasing termination plumbing. Both were grammar-specific in the older elaborator.
No Lean-level rewrite / simp hooks; β/η laws of each connective exist as simp lemmas on the combinators, but the DSL does not surface them.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are all deliberate omissions — the LinearElab elaborator is the minimal, category-polymorphic core. The grammar-specific pieces live in the older Elab/ tree and compose with these combinators via instances on Grammar.

fr:title.text: Validate genericity in a non-grammars category

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Validate genericity in a non-grammars category

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Once Parameterize the elaborator over the target category lands, exercise the generic interface by elaborating the same surface DSL into at least one non-grammars instance — candidates include a free monoidal biclosed category, a presheaf category \hat {\mathcal {C}} on some small \mathcal {C}, or a syntactic category from a different domain.

The point is to catch leakage of grammars-specific assumptions (e.g. concatenation, splittings, String indexing) that the abstract interface failed to hide. Examples should be small but should hit each connective.

fr:title.text: Parameterize the elaborator over the target category

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parameterize the elaborator over the target category

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current sketch hardwires the target: Grammar = String → Type, A ⊢ B = ∀ w, A w → B w, tensor as splittings, etc. Refactor so the elaborator emits terms in an abstract categorical interface — a typeclass packaging the structure required by each connective (monoidal biclosed, finite (co)products, indexed (co)products, initial algebras for grammar_inductive, the LNL adjunction once Embed the full linear / non-linear DSL lands, etc.).

Recover the existing grammars semantics as one instance of this interface. Track exactly which connectives need which structure so users can elaborate fragments of the DSL in categories that don't satisfy the full bill.

fr:title.text: Embed the full linear / non-linear DSL

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Embed the full linear / non-linear DSL

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current sketch elaborates only the ordered linear fragment. Extend the surface syntax and elaborator to cover the full linear / non-linear calculus: a non-linear (intuitionistic) zone alongside the ordered linear zone, with the appropriate adjoint modalities mediating between them.

Concretely: surface-level binders for non-linear variables, weakening / contraction allowed in the non-linear zone only, and elaboration rules for the modalities (e.g. F ⊣ G or ! ⊣ ? in DILL/LNL style — exact form to be settled in the spec subtask). Without this, the DSL cannot express the dependent fragment, since dependency is on non-linear data.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Pin down the on-paper Lambek^D syntax and its Lean target

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Write down the canonical on-paper presentation of Dependent Lambek Calculus that the Lean DSL is intended to embed: judgements, contexts (linear / ordered / non-linear zones), and the formation / introduction / elimination rules for each connective.

For each rule, specify the target Lean term it should elaborate to under the shallow embedding (grammars as String → Type, morphisms as ∀ w, A w → B w). This is the spec the elaborator is implementing — without it the audit in Audit the existing Lean elaborator sketch and the rewrite in Reconstruct the elaborator from spec have no reference point.
